findings.title: Notes stored unencrypted on device
findings.description: The client stores `notes.db` in cleartext with only default file permissions; if the device is stolen or compromised, all notes are readable, violating confidentiality.

findings.title: Random 32‑bit client note IDs risk collisions
findings.description: Note IDs are generated as random 32‑bit integers on the client; collisions across devices could cause duplicate IDs, leading to lost updates or incorrect mapping on the server.

findings.title: Unbounded outbox size can exhaust client and server resources
findings.description: The outbox table has no cap; a device staying offline can accumulate arbitrarily many rows, causing a single sync POST to be extremely large, potentially exceeding request size limits and causing server OOM.

findings.title: Sync POST sends entire outbox in one request
findings.description: The sync protocol transmits the whole outbox batch in a single POST, which combined with an unbounded outbox can produce megabyte‑scale payloads, increasing latency and risk of request failure.

findings.title: Server lacks request timeout for sync
findings.description: The server allows sync requests to run indefinitely; a large or stalled request can tie up server resources, leading to denial‑of‑service.

findings.title: No per‑user rate limiting on sync
findings.description: A misbehaving client can issue sync requests in a tight loop, overwhelming the server because there is no rate limit.

findings.title: Clock‑skew‑based conflict resolution can lose data
findings.description: When two sides edit the same note, the version with the newer client `modified_at` wins; since `modified_at` is the client’s wall clock, clock skew can cause the older edit to be incorrectly discarded.

findings.title: Sync batches lack device attribution
findings.description: The server does not record which device sent each batch, making it difficult to trace misbehaving clients or diagnose data inconsistencies.

findings.title: Silent client sync failures are not alertable
findings.description: Clients that never manage to sync generate no alertable signal; only support tickets surface the issue, delaying detection.

findings.title: Backup restore procedure not rehearsed
findings.description: The design acknowledges that restores have not been rehearsed, leaving the team untested for catastrophic database loss, which risks prolonged downtime or data loss.

findings.title: Unlimited note body size can cause oversized sync payloads
findings.description: Notes have no length cap; a user could create extremely large note bodies, inflating the outbox and sync request size, leading to performance degradation or request failures.

findings.title: Random 32‑bit client‑generated note IDs risk collisions
findings.description: Note `id` is generated on the device as a random 32‑bit integer (line 24). With many users and notes, the probability of a collision grows, which could cause two distinct notes to be treated as the same record, leading to silent overwrites and data loss.

findings.title: Conflict resolution based on client wall‑clock timestamps can lose edits
findings.description: When both client and server edit the same note, the copy with the newer `modified_at` (client wall‑clock) wins (lines 61‑63). Devices with skewed clocks can falsely appear newer, causing legitimate edits to be discarded without any merge UI.

findings.title: SQLite notes database stored unencrypted with default file permissions
findings.description: `notes.db` is written in clear text to the application's data directory (lines 37‑39). On a lost or stolen device, an attacker can read all user notes, violating privacy expectations.

findings.title: Deleted notes retained forever, growing storage and reducing privacy
findings.description: Rows with `deleted = true` are never purged (lines 152‑155). Over time the table will bloat, and deleted user content remains indefinitely, which may conflict with data‑retention policies or privacy regulations.

findings.title: No audit trail of sync operations or device provenance
findings.description: The server does not record which device sent which batch (lines 159‑160). This hampers debugging, forensic analysis, and compliance reporting.

findings.title: Unbounded outbox growth on long‑term offline devices
findings.description: The outbox table has no cap; a device that stays offline indefinitely accumulates rows (lines 31‑35). This can exhaust local storage and lead to very large sync payloads.
